ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The local Ethics Committee of the university approved the general procedure, which adhered to the ethical standards of the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments.
We recruited N = 133 children between the ages of 3.5 and 4.5 years (M age = 4.05 years, SD age = 0.29), 48.9% were girls.
Participants were recruited through the research unit's database, which includes of parents who had expressed interest in participating in studies with their children.
Parents provided informed consent for participation.
We recruited 3.5 to 4.5-year-olds from a wider Zurich area.

Here, we recruited children living in the wider Zurich area in Switzerland, and we directly quantified the cultural values in children's environments that might have produced these differences, whereas previous research relied on contrasts between specific nations.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: The Interplay between Cultural Diversity and (Over-)Imitation
table.data_collection_started: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions:
This study aims to assess the association between 3.5- to 4.5-year-old children’s parental cultural values and language status, and their over-imitation behaviour. 
Our analyses combine confirmatory and exploratory approaches. 

The main confirmatory research question and hypothesis are:

RQ1: How does parental institutional collectivism influence children's over-imitation behaviour in a goal-directed task?

H1: Children whose caregivers endorse more institutional collectivism are more likely to over-imitate the non-contact actions than children whose caregivers endorse less institutional collectivism.

The main exploratory research questions are: 

EQ1: How do other parental cultural values (on the other dimensions of the GLOBE) influence children's over-imitation behaviour in a goal-directed task?

EQ2: How does the cultural diversity, operationalised as the distance between caregivers’ cultural values, influence children’s over-imitation behaviour in a goal-directed task?

EQ3: How does children’s language status influence their over-imitation behaviour in a goal-directed task?
table.design_dependent_variables:
Dependent Variable: Over-imitation
The over-imitation task measures the level to which children over-imitate the experimenter. We adapted the task from Schleihauf and colleagues, (2018). We used a transparent apparatus consisting of a 20 X 9.5 X 24 cm plexiglas box with a transparent tube containing 2 steel marbles and a rod used to extract them. The tube is closed with a lid on the front, which can be lifted to open. The marbles can be extracted from the tube using a rod with a magnet on the top. On the top surface of the box, a black wooden lever is attached. Besides the box is a transparent square, containing a black button. 

The experimenter told the child she will show them how to retrieve marbles from the special box. She proceeded to show the child an inefficient strategy to obtain the marbles. This strategy includes 4 redundant actions: (1) clapping three times, (2) pushing the lever back and forth, (3) tapping the rod in the palm of the hand three times, (4) using the rod to push the button on the side of the box, and a fifth essential action: inserting the magnetic side of the rod to extract the marble (Schleihauf et al., 2018; Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2021). Only the last step is needed to retrieve the marble. Afterwards, the experimenter put the box in front of the child and told them: “Now it is your turn, you can do it however you like” (in local language). While the child was retrieving the marbles, the experimenter looked away and prepared the next task but stayed present in the room.

The redundant actions are categorised into noncontact actions or instrumental actions (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020). Noncontact actions: action 1 and 3 (clapping and tapping the rod in the palm). Pseudo-instrumental actions: action 2 and 4 (pushing the lever, pushing the button). Children’s performance of these actions and the marble retrieval action is coded from video by a trained coder in a binary manner: 0 = action not performed, 1 = action performed. For the analysis, we will only use the data from the four redundant actions (not marble retrieval).
table.study_design_overview:
This study does not have different conditions. Instead, we use parental cultural values, children’s language status and language entropy as independent variables. In addition, we use children’s age as a control variable. 

Independent Variable: Parental Values
To measure caregivers’ cultural values, we used a subscale of the Global Leadership and Organizational Behavior Effectiveness (GLOBE; House et al., 2004), completed by both caregivers. It assesses how the caregivers generally think the society should be (subscale 3). The subscale consists of 39 questions on a 7-point Likert scale and was administered as an online survey. The subscale measures parental values on the following dimensions: uncertainty avoidance, future orientation, power distance, institutional collectivism, human orientation, performance orientation, ingroup collectivism, gender egalitarianism, and assertiveness. The total score for each caregiver on each dimension is calculated as the sum of all item responses divided by the number of answered questions in each dimension. The final score is calculated as the mean score between both caregivers. In case only one caregiver completed the questionnaire, we will use their score. We will standardise this variable prior to the analysis to have a mean of 0 and SD of 1.   

Independent Variable: Cultural Diversity
To assess differences between caregivers’ values, we will calculate the Euclidean distance score (Carlier et al., 2024) based on their responses to the GLOBE (House et al., 2004). For each cultural dimension, we will compute the absolute difference between the two caregivers’ scores. These differences will then be combined into a single index reflecting the overall discrepancy between caregivers’ cultural values (D): 

D=∑i=1n​(xi​−yi​)2

With i as the assessed cultural dimension and x and y for the cultural values of caregiver 1 and 2 on this dimension. 

We will standardise this variable prior to the analysis to have a mean of 0 and SD of 1. 

Independent Variable: Language Status
In a parental questionnaire (Openscript GmbH, 2025), caregivers were asked for each caregiving situation since the child's birth, for each day of the week, each interaction partner and each language, and the amount of time the child spent with this interaction partner and was exposed to each language. The questionnaire was administered as a web app with a touch screen device, on which caregivers can indicate their child’s weekly schedules or in a pen-and-paper format.

Language status will be determined based on the amount of time the child is exposed to a second language/language variety. All children in our sample are exposed to [blinded for review, language spoken by the majority of the society]. Bilingual children are exposed to a second language for at least 20% of their awake time, and not more than 10% to a third language. Bidialectal children are exposed to [blinded for review, another dialect of the language spoken by the majority of the society] for at least 20% of their awake time, and not more than 10% to a third language. Monolingual children are exposed to [blinded for review, language spoken by the majority of the society] for at least 90% of their awake time. Language status will be contrast coded as –0.5 (monolingual), 0.5 (bilingual) and 0 (bidialectal) for standardisation purposes for the planned analysis.
table.statistical_tests:
We plan to use Bayesian Generalised Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs). The outcome variable is binary (representing the over-imitation behaviour of a child on each redundant action, 0 = non performed, 1 = performed. We will therefore apply a Bernoulli distribution in our modelling framework. We will include random intercepts for each child to account for repeated measurements across trials for each child and action type. All models will be fitted using the brms package (Bürkner, 2017) in R (R Core Team, 2025).

H1: Children whose caregivers endorse more collectivistic cultural values are more likely to over-imitate than children whose caregivers endorse more individualistic values. 

Over-imitation (1/0) ~ institutional collectivism (continuous) + age + action type (pseudo-instrumental/noncontact) + action (step1/2/3/4) + (1 | child)

To answer our exploratory research questions, we will run the following models: 

EQ1: Over-imitation (1/0) ~ parental difference (continuous) + age + action type (pseudo/noncontact) + action (step1/2/3/4) + (1 | child)

For every other cultural dimension: 
EQ2: Over-imitation (1/0) ~ parental values (continuous) + age + action type (pseudo/noncontact) + action (step1/2/3/4) + (1 | child)

EQ3: Over-imitation (1/0) ~ language status (mono/bid/bil) + age + action type (pseudo/noncontact) + action (step1/2/3/4) + (1 | child)

For the fixed effect of language status and parental values, we will use a norm (0,1) prior. For the fixed effect of age, we will use a norm (0,10) prior. For all other effects, we will use default priors in the brms package.

All continuous predictors will be mean-centred and scaled. Categorical predictors will be contrast-coded. 

We will run 4 chains with 2000 iterations each (1000 warm-up) and assess convergence using R-hat statistics (smaller than 1.01) and visual inspection of trace plots. Further, we will perform posterior predictive checks using to ensure model adequacy. If necessary, we will consider alternative model structures or increase the number of chains, the number of iterations, adapt adapt_delta or the max_treedepth values. 

We will use the probability of direction (pd) for the fixed effects as our inference index (Makowski et al., 2019). We will accept our hypotheses if the pd is larger or equal to 0.9.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Children with missing data will be excluded from the respective analysis. Missing data will not be imputed.

Exclusion criteria
We will exclude participants from the analyses that include parental difference if only one caregiver completed the GLOBE, as no difference score can be computed. 
We will exclude participants from the analyses that include language status if the calculation of children’s language exposure from the language exposure questionnaire shows they do not fulfil the criteria for monolingualism, bilingualism or bidialectalism (see 3.) or if we cannot calculate their language exposure (e.g. due to corrupted files or unfulfilled language exposure questionnaire). We will exclude participants from the entire analysis in case the video recording of the session is unavailable or corrupted, or when the experimenter judges after the session that the participant did not understand enough [blinded for review, language spoken by the majority of the society] to understand the procedure. Further, we will exclude participants who do not complete the over-imitation task or in case a caregiver or sibling interferes, or the experimenter makes an error in the procedure that interferes with the task delivery.
table.sample_size: We recruited 133 children between the ages of 3.5 and 4.5 years across different language groups (monolingual/bidialectal/bilingual). The sample size is based on a Bayesian Optional Stopping design (Mani et al., 2021; Schönbrodt et al., 2017) used in the MINION (pragMatIcs iN cOmmunIcatioN) study, preregistered under https://osf.io/hgr98/overview?view_only=8c2484c223754b89b7d8ed80e35317d8.
table.additional_comments:
Additional analyses
Additionally, we will explore whether a family’s language status is associated with differences in caregivers’ cultural values. 

EQ4: How does the family’s language status influence differences between caregivers’ cultural values?

table.research_questions:
This study aims to assess the association between 3.5- to 4.5-year-old children’s parental cultural values and language status, and their over-imitation behaviour. 
Our analyses combine confirmatory and exploratory approaches. 

The main confirmatory research question and hypothesis are:

RQ1: How does parental institutional collectivism influence children's over-imitation behaviour in a goal-directed task?

H1: Children whose caregivers endorse more institutional collectivism are more likely to over-imitate the non-contact actions than children whose caregivers endorse less institutional collectivism.

The main exploratory research questions are: 

EQ1: How do other parental cultural values (on the other dimensions of the GLOBE) influence children's over-imitation behaviour in a goal-directed task?

EQ2: How does the cultural diversity, operationalised as the distance between caregivers’ cultural values, influence children’s over-imitation behaviour in a goal-directed task?

EQ3: How does children’s language status influence their over-imitation behaviour in a goal-directed task?
table.design_dependent_variables:
Dependent Variable: Over-imitation
The over-imitation task measures the level to which children over-imitate the experimenter. We adapted the task from Schleihauf and colleagues, (2018). We used a transparent apparatus consisting of a 20 X 9.5 X 24 cm plexiglas box with a transparent tube containing 2 steel marbles and a rod used to extract them. The tube is closed with a lid on the front, which can be lifted to open. The marbles can be extracted from the tube using a rod with a magnet on the top. On the top surface of the box, a black wooden lever is attached. Besides the box is a transparent square, containing a black button. 

The experimenter told the child she will show them how to retrieve marbles from the special box. She proceeded to show the child an inefficient strategy to obtain the marbles. This strategy includes 4 redundant actions: (1) clapping three times, (2) pushing the lever back and forth, (3) tapping the rod in the palm of the hand three times, (4) using the rod to push the button on the side of the box, and a fifth essential action: inserting the magnetic side of the rod to extract the marble (Schleihauf et al., 2018; Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2021). Only the last step is needed to retrieve the marble. Afterwards, the experimenter put the box in front of the child and told them: “Now it is your turn, you can do it however you like” (in local language). While the child was retrieving the marbles, the experimenter looked away and prepared the next task but stayed present in the room.

The redundant actions are categorised into noncontact actions or instrumental actions (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020). Noncontact actions: action 1 and 3 (clapping and tapping the rod in the palm). Pseudo-instrumental actions: action 2 and 4 (pushing the lever, pushing the button). Children’s performance of these actions and the marble retrieval action is coded from video by a trained coder in a binary manner: 0 = action not performed, 1 = action performed. For the analysis, we will only use the data from the four redundant actions (not marble retrieval).
table.study_design_overview:
This study does not have different conditions. Instead, we use parental cultural values, children’s language status and language entropy as independent variables. In addition, we use children’s age as a control variable. 

Independent Variable: Parental Values
To measure caregivers’ cultural values, we used a subscale of the Global Leadership and Organizational Behavior Effectiveness (GLOBE; House et al., 2004), completed by both caregivers. It assesses how the caregivers generally think the society should be (subscale 3). The subscale consists of 39 questions on a 7-point Likert scale and was administered as an online survey. The subscale measures parental values on the following dimensions: uncertainty avoidance, future orientation, power distance, institutional collectivism, human orientation, performance orientation, ingroup collectivism, gender egalitarianism, and assertiveness. The total score for each caregiver on each dimension is calculated as the sum of all item responses divided by the number of answered questions in each dimension. The final score is calculated as the mean score between both caregivers. In case only one caregiver completed the questionnaire, we will use their score. We will standardise this variable prior to the analysis to have a mean of 0 and SD of 1.   

Independent Variable: Cultural Diversity
To assess differences between caregivers’ values, we will calculate the Euclidean distance score (Carlier et al., 2024) based on their responses to the GLOBE (House et al., 2004). For each cultural dimension, we will compute the absolute difference between the two caregivers’ scores. These differences will then be combined into a single index reflecting the overall discrepancy between caregivers’ cultural values (D): 

D=∑i=1n​(xi​−yi​)2

With i as the assessed cultural dimension and x and y for the cultural values of caregiver 1 and 2 on this dimension. 

We will standardise this variable prior to the analysis to have a mean of 0 and SD of 1. 

Independent Variable: Language Status
In a parental questionnaire (Openscript GmbH, 2025), caregivers were asked for each caregiving situation since the child's birth, for each day of the week, each interaction partner and each language, and the amount of time the child spent with this interaction partner and was exposed to each language. The questionnaire was administered as a web app with a touch screen device, on which caregivers can indicate their child’s weekly schedules or in a pen-and-paper format.

Language status will be determined based on the amount of time the child is exposed to a second language/language variety. All children in our sample are exposed to [blinded for review, language spoken by the majority of the society]. Bilingual children are exposed to a second language for at least 20% of their awake time, and not more than 10% to a third language. Bidialectal children are exposed to [blinded for review, another dialect of the language spoken by the majority of the society] for at least 20% of their awake time, and not more than 10% to a third language. Monolingual children are exposed to [blinded for review, language spoken by the majority of the society] for at least 90% of their awake time. Language status will be contrast coded as –0.5 (monolingual), 0.5 (bilingual) and 0 (bidialectal) for standardisation purposes for the planned analysis.
table.statistical_tests:
We plan to use Bayesian Generalised Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs). The outcome variable is binary (representing the over-imitation behaviour of a child on each redundant action, 0 = non performed, 1 = performed. We will therefore apply a Bernoulli distribution in our modelling framework. We will include random intercepts for each child to account for repeated measurements across trials for each child and action type. All models will be fitted using the brms package (Bürkner, 2017) in R (R Core Team, 2025).

H1: Children whose caregivers endorse more collectivistic cultural values are more likely to over-imitate than children whose caregivers endorse more individualistic values. 

Over-imitation (1/0) ~ institutional collectivism (continuous) + age + action type (pseudo-instrumental/noncontact) + action (step1/2/3/4) + (1 | child)

To answer our exploratory research questions, we will run the following models: 

EQ1: Over-imitation (1/0) ~ parental difference (continuous) + age + action type (pseudo/noncontact) + action (step1/2/3/4) + (1 | child)

For every other cultural dimension: 
EQ2: Over-imitation (1/0) ~ parental values (continuous) + age + action type (pseudo/noncontact) + action (step1/2/3/4) + (1 | child)

EQ3: Over-imitation (1/0) ~ language status (mono/bid/bil) + age + action type (pseudo/noncontact) + action (step1/2/3/4) + (1 | child)

For the fixed effect of language status and parental values, we will use a norm (0,1) prior. For the fixed effect of age, we will use a norm (0,10) prior. For all other effects, we will use default priors in the brms package.

All continuous predictors will be mean-centred and scaled. Categorical predictors will be contrast-coded. 

We will run 4 chains with 2000 iterations each (1000 warm-up) and assess convergence using R-hat statistics (smaller than 1.01) and visual inspection of trace plots. Further, we will perform posterior predictive checks using to ensure model adequacy. If necessary, we will consider alternative model structures or increase the number of chains, the number of iterations, adapt adapt_delta or the max_treedepth values. 

We will use the probability of direction (pd) for the fixed effects as our inference index (Makowski et al., 2019). We will accept our hypotheses if the pd is larger or equal to 0.9.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Children with missing data will be excluded from the respective analysis. Missing data will not be imputed.

Exclusion criteria
We will exclude participants from the analyses that include parental difference if only one caregiver completed the GLOBE, as no difference score can be computed. 
We will exclude participants from the analyses that include language status if the calculation of children’s language exposure from the language exposure questionnaire shows they do not fulfil the criteria for monolingualism, bilingualism or bidialectalism (see 3.) or if we cannot calculate their language exposure (e.g. due to corrupted files or unfulfilled language exposure questionnaire). We will exclude participants from the entire analysis in case the video recording of the session is unavailable or corrupted, or when the experimenter judges after the session that the participant did not understand enough [blinded for review, language spoken by the majority of the society] to understand the procedure. Further, we will exclude participants who do not complete the over-imitation task or in case a caregiver or sibling interferes, or the experimenter makes an error in the procedure that interferes with the task delivery.

Afterwards, the experimenter put the box in front of the child and told them: “Now it is your turn, you can do it however you like” (in local language). While the child was retrieving the marbles, the experimenter looked away and prepared the next task but stayed present in the room.

The redundant actions are categorised into noncontact actions or instrumental actions (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020). Noncontact actions: action 1 and 3 (clapping and tapping the rod in the palm). Pseudo-instrumental actions: action 2 and 4 (pushing the lever, pushing the button). Children’s performance of these actions and the marble retrieval action is coded from video by a trained coder in a binary manner: 0 = action not performed, 1 = action performed. For the analysis, we will only use the data from the four redundant actions (not marble retrieval).", "This study does not have different conditions. Instead, we use parental cultural values, children’s language status and language entropy as independent variables. In addition, we use children’s age as a control variable.

Independent Variable: Parental Values
To measure caregivers’ cultural values, we used a subscale of the Global Leadership and Organizational Behavior Effectiveness (GLOBE; House et al., 2004), completed by both caregivers. It assesses how the caregivers generally think the society should be (subscale 3). The subscale consists of 39 questions on a 7-point Likert scale and was administered as an online survey. The subscale measures parental values on the following dimensions: uncertainty avoidance, future orientation, power distance, institutional collectivism, human orientation, performance orientation, ingroup collectivism, gender egalitarianism, and assertiveness. The total score for each caregiver on each dimension is calculated as the sum of all item responses divided by the number of answered questions in each dimension. The final score is calculated as the mean score between both caregivers. In case only one caregiver completed the questionnaire, we will use their score. We will standardise this variable prior to the analysis to have a mean of 0 and SD of 1.

Independent Variable: Cultural Diversity
To assess differences between caregivers’ values, we will calculate the Euclidean distance score (Carlier et al., 2024) based on their responses to the GLOBE (House et al., 2004). For each cultural dimension, we will compute the absolute difference between the two caregivers’ scores. These differences will then be combined into a single index reflecting the overall discrepancy between caregivers’ cultural values (D):

D=∑i=1n​(xi​−yi​)2

With i as the assessed cultural dimension and x and y for the cultural values of caregiver 1 and 2 on this dimension.

We will standardise this variable prior to the analysis to have a mean of 0 and SD of 1.

Independent Variable: Language Status
In a parental questionnaire (Openscript GmbH, 2025), caregivers were asked for each caregiving situation since the child's birth, for each day of the week, each interaction partner and each language, and the amount of time the child spent with this interaction partner and was exposed to each language. The questionnaire was administered as a web app with a touch screen device, on which caregivers can indicate their child’s weekly schedules or in a pen-and-paper format.

Language status will be determined based on the amount of time the child is exposed to a second language/language variety. All children in our sample are exposed to [blinded for review, language spoken by the majority of the society]. Bilingual children are exposed to a second language for at least 20% of their awake time, and not more than 10% to a third language. Bidialectal children are exposed to [blinded for review, another dialect of the language spoken by the majority of the society] for at least 20% of their awake time, and not more than 10% to a third language. Monolingual children are exposed to [blinded for review, language spoken by the majority of the society] for at least 90% of their awake time. Language status will be contrast coded as –0.5 (monolingual), 0.5 (bilingual) and 0 (bidialectal) for standardisation purposes for the planned analysis.", "We plan to use Bayesian Generalised Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs). The outcome variable is binary (representing the over-imitation behaviour of a child on each redundant action, 0 = non performed, 1 = performed. We will therefore apply a Bernoulli distribution in our modelling framework. We will include random intercepts for each child to account for repeated measurements across trials for each child and action type. All models will be fitted using the brms package (Bürkner, 2017) in R (R Core Team, 2025).

H1: Children whose caregivers endorse more collectivistic cultural values are more likely to over-imitate than children whose caregivers endorse more individualistic values.

Over-imitation (1/0) ~ institutional collectivism (continuous) + age + action type (pseudo-instrumental/noncontact) + action (step1/2/3/4) + (1 | child)

To answer our exploratory research questions, we will run the following models:

EQ1: Over-imitation (1/0) ~ parental difference (continuous) + age + action type (pseudo/noncontact) + action (step1/2/3/4) + (1 | child)

For every other cultural dimension:
EQ2: Over-imitation (1/0) ~ parental values (continuous) + age + action type (pseudo/noncontact) + action (step1/2/3/4) + (1 | child)

For the fixed effect of language status and parental values, we will use a norm (0,1) prior. For the fixed effect of age, we will use a norm (0,10) prior. For all other effects, we will use default priors in the brms package.

All continuous predictors will be mean-centred and scaled. Categorical predictors will be contrast-coded.

We will run 4 chains with 2000 iterations each (1000 warm-up) and assess convergence using R-hat statistics (smaller than 1.01) and visual inspection of trace plots. Further, we will perform posterior predictive checks using to ensure model adequacy. If necessary, we will consider alternative model structures or increase the number of chains, the number of iterations, adapt adapt_delta or the max_treedepth values.

We will use the probability of direction (pd) for the fixed effects as our inference index (Makowski et al., 2019). We will accept our hypotheses if the pd is larger or equal to 0.9.", "Children with missing data will be excluded from the respective analysis. Missing data will not be imputed.

Exclusion criteria
We will exclude participants from the analyses that include parental difference if only one caregiver completed the GLOBE, as no difference score can be computed.
We will exclude participants from the analyses that include language status if the calculation of children’s language exposure from the language exposure questionnaire shows they do not fulfil the criteria for monolingualism, bilingualism or bidialectalism (see 3.) or if we cannot calculate their language exposure (e.g. due to corrupted files or unfulfilled language exposure questionnaire). :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 234 columns across 10 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 10 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: We recruited N = 133 children between the ages of 3.5 and 4.5 years (M age = 4.05 years, SD age = 0.29), 48.9% were girls.
Participants were recruited through the research unit's database, which includes of parents who had expressed interest in participating in studies with their children.
Parents provided informed consent for participation.
We recruited 3.5 to 4.5-year-olds from a wider Zurich area.

Here, we recruited children living in the wider Zurich area in Switzerland, and we directly quantified the cultural values in children's environments that might have produced these differences, whereas previous research relied on contrasts between specific nations.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

#### File paths

**4 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `globe_raw.csv` to `../Data/globe_raw.csv` (in globe_recoding.r); `overimitation_raw.csv` to `../Data/overimitation_raw.csv` (in overimitation_preprocessing_osf.r); `overimitation_data_preprocessed.csv` to `../Data/overimitation_data_preprocessed.csv` (in bayesian_analysis_osf.r); `globe_data_wide.csv` to `../Data/globe_data_wide.csv` (in bayesian_analysis_osf.r). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 2 ran without error, 0 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: Acknowledgements: We thank the Kleine Weltentdecker*innen Lab and the Jacobs Center for Productive Youth Development at Universität Zürich for providing the resources necessary to this research and all children and their caregivers for their participation in our studies.

We would like to thank both reviewers for their helpful commentary, and in particular Reviewer 1 for helpful suggestions on how the study's results could be used to extend the Dual-Process Perspective on over-imitation.
Imitation is one of the most important learning avenues for humans.
It is fundamental to our species' ability to accumulate culture across generations (Heyes, 2001).
text.formatted: It is fundamental to our species' ability to accumulate culture across generations <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Heyes, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Imitation is defined by copying the actions or behaviours of an observed model (Legare & Nielsen, 2015).
text.formatted: Imitation is defined by copying the actions or behaviours of an observed model <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Legare & Nielsen, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Children use imitation in everyday life and at various levels (Heyes, 2001; Nielsen & Tomaselli, 2010): it underlies their acquisition of motor actions and practical skills (Ledford & Wolery, 2011), instrumental tool use (Legare & Nielsen, 2015), language (Klinger et al., 2016), and the transmission of customs and norms (Over & Carpenter, 2013).
text.formatted: Children use imitation in everyday life and at various levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Heyes, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Nielsen & Tomaselli, 2010)</ref>: it underlies their acquisition of motor actions and practical skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Ledford & Wolery, 2011)</ref>, instrumental tool use <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Legare & Nielsen, 2015)</ref>, language <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Klinger et al., 2016)</ref>, and the transmission of customs and norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Over & Carpenter, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This makes it a vital part of early development (Carpenter & Nielsen, 2008).
text.formatted: This makes it a vital part of early development <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Carpenter & Nielsen, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Given the importance of imitation to our species and to individual development, researchers strive to explain how and when it emerges, and under what circumstances.
Imitation also occurs when we are not explicitly trying to achieve a certain goal.
Humans tend to imitate others' behaviour, even when their goal is unclear.
This phenomenon is known as over-imitation (Hoehl et al., 2019) and is observed in both children and adults (Horner & Whiten, 2005; McGuigan et al., 2011 McGuigan et al., , 2012)).
text.formatted: This phenomenon is known as over-imitation <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hoehl et al., 2019)</ref> and is observed in both children and adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Horner & Whiten, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">McGuigan et al., 2011</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">McGuigan et al., , 2012))</ref>.

text.text: Over-imitation has been reported across different cultures, although its extent varies (Nielsen & Tomaselli, 2010; Stengelin et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Over-imitation has been reported across different cultures, although its extent varies <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Nielsen & Tomaselli, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Stengelin et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, children from more collectivistic cultural backgrounds over-imitate more than children from individualistic ones (Clegg & Legare, 2016; Fong et al., 2021), and over-imitation rates differ between Western, first nation, and Bushmen children (Nielsen et al., 2014), which we discuss in detail below.
text.formatted: For instance, children from more collectivistic cultural backgrounds over-imitate more than children from individualistic ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clegg & Legare, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Fong et al., 2021)</ref>, and over-imitation rates differ between Western, first nation, and Bushmen children <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Nielsen et al., 2014</ref>), which we discuss in detail below.

text.text: To study over-imitation, participants, usually children, observe a series of unnecessary actions followed by a single action necessary to achieve a goal.
After this observation phase, they are given the opportunity to act independently.
Over-imitation is evident in children's performance of unnecessary actions, and how many of these are performed varies systematically across individuals and contexts (Hoehl et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Over-imitation is evident in children's performance of unnecessary actions, and how many of these are performed varies systematically across individuals and contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hoehl et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: A common paradigm to study over-imitation involves retrieving a reward from an object, such as a puzzle box (Horner & Whiten, 2005), although paradigms vary widely and include, for instance, imitation of unnecessary steps in everyday tasks and social interactions (Legare & Nielsen, 2015).
text.formatted: A common paradigm to study over-imitation involves retrieving a reward from an object, such as a puzzle box <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Horner & Whiten, 2005)</ref>, although paradigms vary widely and include, for instance, imitation of unnecessary steps in everyday tasks and social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Legare & Nielsen, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The mechanisms underlying over-imitation can be grouped into causal, affiliative, and normative processes (Hoehl et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The mechanisms underlying over-imitation can be grouped into causal, affiliative, and normative processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hoehl et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Causal processes occur when people assume that others' actions have a purpose, even if this purpose is unclear to them.
These are supported by findings that children selectively omit accidental actions (Gardiner, 2014; Lyons et al., 2011) and are sensitive to whether a model acts intentionally (Gergely et al., 2002).
text.formatted: These are supported by findings that children selectively omit accidental actions <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Gardiner, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Lyons et al., 2011)</ref> and are sensitive to whether a model acts intentionally <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gergely et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Affiliative processes occur when people copy others' actions because they want to affiliate with them, as imitation can signal social alignment and strengthen interpersonal bonds.
Children over-imitate more, when a familiar, in-group model demonstrates actions (Buttelmann et al., 2013; Nielsen & Blank, 2011) and when they are being observed (Stengelin et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Children over-imitate more, when a familiar, in-group model demonstrates actions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Buttelmann et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Nielsen & Blank, 2011)</ref> and when they are being observed <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Stengelin et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Normative explanations propose that individuals treat demonstrated actions as socially prescribed, assuming that even unnecessary steps are part of the social norms -a conventional or "correct" behaviour.
For example, not only do children reproduce unnecessary actions themselves, but they also expect third parties to do so and protest when they do not (Kenward, 2012; Keupp et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For example, not only do children reproduce unnecessary actions themselves, but they also expect third parties to do so and protest when they do not <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Kenward, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Keupp et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: All three processes have been systematically shown to be involved in why we over-imitate (Hoehl et al., 2019).
text.formatted: All three processes have been systematically shown to be involved in why we over-imitate <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hoehl et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, children do not imitate irrelevant actions that are accidental or unintentional (Gardiner, 2014; Lyons et al., 2011), suggesting they actively infer intent.
text.formatted: For instance, children do not imitate irrelevant actions that are accidental or unintentional <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Gardiner, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Lyons et al., 2011)</ref>, suggesting they actively infer intent.

text.text: For intentional actions, children still over-imitate even when they are not being observed and are explicitly told they will get a reward regardless (Hoehl et al., 2014; Schleihauf et al., 2018), or when they are unaware of participating in an experiment at all (Whiten et al., 2016).
text.formatted: For intentional actions, children still over-imitate even when they are not being observed and are explicitly told they will get a reward regardless <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hoehl et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Schleihauf et al., 2018)</ref>, or when they are unaware of participating in an experiment at all <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Whiten et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that over-imitation reflects an interaction between cognitive inference, social motivation, and sensitivity to cultural norms.
Age-related changes influence the extent to which children reproduce irrelevant actions.

In the second year of life, children do not yet over-imitate, but they are already selective in their copying of others' behaviour: They imitate models differently based on their group membership (Buttelmann et al., 2013), confidence (Birch et al., 2010), age (Zmyj, Aschersleben, et al., 2012; Zmyj, Daum, et al., 2012), competence (Crivello et al., 2018; Zmyj et al., 2010), the inferred rationality of others' actions (Gergely & Csibra, 2003; Gergely et al., 2002), the salience of context stimuli (Beisert et al., 2012), and their motor resonance (Paulus et al., 2011, mapping others' actions onto their own motor repertoire).
text.formatted: In the second year of life, children do not yet over-imitate, but they are already selective in their copying of others' behaviour: They imitate models differently based on their group membership <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Buttelmann et al., 2013)</ref>, confidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Birch et al., 2010)</ref>, age <ref type="bibr">(Zmyj, Aschersleben, et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zmyj, Daum, et al., 2012)</ref>, competence <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Crivello et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Zmyj et al., 2010)</ref>, the inferred rationality of others' actions <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Gergely & Csibra, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Gergely et al., 2002)</ref>, the salience of context stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Beisert et al., 2012)</ref>, and their motor resonance <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Paulus et al., 2011</ref>, mapping others' actions onto their own motor repertoire).

text.text: A developmental shift occurs in the second year of infants' lives, as they become increasingly likely to copy others' actions regardless of their causal relevance (Brugger et al., 2007; Gellén & Buttelmann, 2019; Hilbrink et al., 2013).
text.formatted: A developmental shift occurs in the second year of infants' lives, as they become increasingly likely to copy others' actions regardless of their causal relevance <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brugger et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Gellén & Buttelmann, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Hilbrink et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Children's over-imitation increases between the ages of 3 and 8 (Stengelin et al., 2019). Clay et al. (2018) showed with 4-to 6-year-old children that these age-related changes in over-imitation likely reflect the changing underlying processes.
text.formatted: Children's over-imitation increases between the ages of 3 and 8 <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Stengelin et al., 2019)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Clay et al. (2018)</ref> showed with 4-to 6-year-old children that these age-related changes in over-imitation likely reflect the changing underlying processes.

text.text: Younger children were more likely to over-imitate when the unnecessary actions were framed as instrumental (causally relevant), whereas older children were more likely to over-imitate when the unnecessary actions were framed as normative.

In addition, younger children were more likely to reproduce the actions performed on or in contact with the puzzle box rather than other actions, compared to older children, likely because they perceive object-bound actions as more causally relevant (Clay et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In addition, younger children were more likely to reproduce the actions performed on or in contact with the puzzle box rather than other actions, compared to older children, likely because they perceive object-bound actions as more causally relevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clay et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This demonstrates that with age, the relative importance of the mechanisms underlying over-imitation changes: children's tendency to over-imitate increasingly reflects sensitivity to the social (Nielsen & Blank, 2011) and normative context of the demonstration (Kenward, 2012) rather than assumptions about causality.
text.formatted: This demonstrates that with age, the relative importance of the mechanisms underlying over-imitation changes: children's tendency to over-imitate increasingly reflects sensitivity to the social <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Nielsen & Blank, 2011)</ref> and normative context of the demonstration <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Kenward, 2012)</ref> rather than assumptions about causality.

text.text: Therefore, children's growing understanding of social conventions and their increasing awareness of others' expectations increase the role of normative and affiliative motivations for over-imitation with age.

Early theoretical accounts of over-imitation stress its two main functions: instrumental (to learn something new; Lyons et al., 2007 Lyons et al., , 2011;; Whiten et al., 2009) and social (to affiliate or adhere to social norms; Over & Carpenter, 2013).
text.formatted: Early theoretical accounts of over-imitation stress its two main functions: instrumental (to learn something new; <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Lyons et al., 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Lyons et al., , 2011;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Whiten et al., 2009)</ref> and social (to affiliate or adhere to social norms; <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Over & Carpenter, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The dual-process perspective on over-imitation aims to unify those explanations, and place them in the context of children's development (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020).
text.formatted: The dual-process perspective on over-imitation aims to unify those explanations, and place them in the context of children's development <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: It explains over-imitation behaviour of children in different contexts and situations.
Whether children over-imitate or not is based on the interaction between two distinct types of processing: type 1 and type 2.
Blanket copying, based on type 1 processing, is quick and low in cognitive effort.
It occurs when children imitate others' unnecessary actions without explicitly questioning their causal relevance or motivation.
Under certain circumstances, blanket copying can be overridden when children are prompted to question whether demonstrated actions are necessary.
In such cases, children engage in deliberate considerations of whether or not to copy, based on type 2 processing, which is slower and requires more cognitive effort.
Type 2 processing is triggered when the observer recognises that the actions he or she observed were causally irrelevant.

This can happen in a number of ways: by observing an efficient strategy after seeing a demonstration that included unnecessary actions, or by observing actions that did not involve contact with the puzzle box (non-contact actions, e.g. clapping), which are clearly recognisable as causally irrelevant.

In contrast, observing pseudo-instrumental actions (actions that look instrumental, but are not; e.g., pressing a button) is more likely to lead to type 1 processing because they can be easily mistaken for instrumental actions.

To sum up, the dual-process perspective on over-imitation posits that observation of unnecessary actions might lead to either type 1 or type 2 processing, depending on the context and the types of actions being observed.
Triggering children's type 2 processing leads to deliberate considerations whether or not to copy (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020).
text.formatted: Triggering children's type 2 processing leads to deliberate considerations whether or not to copy <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Different factors might influence this consideration at different levels.

External factors such as demonstration context (e.g., instrumental or normative instructions; Legare et al., 2015), setting, such as the environment (e.g., experimental or natural setting; Whiten et al., 2016), or others' behaviour (e.g., being observed or not; Marsh et al., 2019) may shape the goals children hold in a given situation or interaction.
text.formatted: External factors such as demonstration context (e.g., instrumental or normative instructions; <ref type="bibr">Legare et al., 2015)</ref>, setting, such as the environment (e.g., experimental or natural setting; <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Whiten et al., 2016)</ref>, or others' behaviour (e.g., being observed or not; <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Marsh et al., 2019)</ref> may shape the goals children hold in a given situation or interaction.

text.text: These individual goals (e.g., instrumental, normative, affiliative, or entertainment goals; Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2021) then shape children's decision on whether or not to copy.
text.formatted: These individual goals (e.g., instrumental, normative, affiliative, or entertainment goals; <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2021)</ref> then shape children's decision on whether or not to copy.

text.text: Individual factors such as personality or personal values (Flynn & Whiten, 2012; Hilbrink et al., 2013)
text.formatted: Individual factors such as personality or personal values <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Flynn & Whiten, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Hilbrink et al., 2013)</ref>

text.text: Over-imitation is a universal phenomenon, but the extent to which children over-imitate differs between cultures (Berl & Hewlett, 2015; Clegg & Legare, 2016; Fong et al., 2021; Nielsen & Tomaselli, 2010; Nielsen et al., 2014; Stengelin et al., 2019 Stengelin et al., , 2020)).
text.formatted: Over-imitation is a universal phenomenon, but the extent to which children over-imitate differs between cultures <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Berl & Hewlett, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Clegg & Legare, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Fong et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Nielsen & Tomaselli, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Nielsen et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Stengelin et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Stengelin et al., , 2020))</ref>.

text.text: This line of research relied on cross-cultural comparisons.

For instance, 6-to 8-year-old children from a Western, individualist culture (United States) over-imitated less than children from a non-Western, collectivist culture (Vanuatu, Melanesian archipelago), when the task was placed in an instrumental, but not normative, context (Clegg & Legare, 2016).
text.formatted: For instance, 6-to 8-year-old children from a Western, individualist culture (United States) over-imitated less than children from a non-Western, collectivist culture (Vanuatu, Melanesian archipelago), when the task was placed in an instrumental, but not normative, context <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clegg & Legare, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Even though the children from both groups were likely able to realise that the unnecessary actions were causally irrelevant, children from a more collectivist culture showed more normative motivation to copy the actions than children from an individualist culture.
When the goals of the task were made explicitly normative, children from an individualist culture over-imitated to the same, greater extent as the children from a collectivist culture.

Similarly, 4-to 6-year-old children from a rural, indigenous community in Malaysia over-imitated more than children from an urban city in Australia, and a peri-urban township in Malaysia (Fong et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Similarly, 4-to 6-year-old children from a rural, indigenous community in Malaysia over-imitated more than children from an urban city in Australia, and a peri-urban township in Malaysia <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Fong et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This effect was attributed to the stronger conformity preference in the rural community, which increased children's normative goals to copy.
Thus, cultural values within children's communities can influence their over-imitation by affecting whether they have normative goals to copy.

The aforementioned studies compared groups defined by geography or ethnicity, leaving open the question of which specific cultural values drive these differences and how they vary at the individual level.
The present study addresses this by measuring parents' individual cultural values directly using the GLOBE framework (House et al., 2004).
text.formatted: The present study addresses this by measuring parents' individual cultural values directly using the GLOBE framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(House et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The GLOBE framework assesses nine cultural dimensions, including institutional collectivism (the belief that societal institutions should promote collective action) and in-group collectivism (the belief that families and close groups should be characterised by loyalty and group pride).
See Table 1 for definitions and example questions of all nine dimensions assessed.
text.formatted: See Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> for definitions and example questions of all nine dimensions assessed.

text.text: Prior work showed that institutional collectivism is linked to how children respond to norm violations (Gampe & Daum, 2018): children of parents with higher institutional collectivism responded less saliently to norm violations, suggesting their norm enforcement operates more implicitly.
text.formatted: Prior work showed that institutional collectivism is linked to how children respond to norm violations <ref type="bibr">(Gampe & Daum, 2018)</ref>: children of parents with higher institutional collectivism responded less saliently to norm violations, suggesting their norm enforcement operates more implicitly.

text.text: For this reason, we focused in the present study primarily on specific cultural aspects of collectivism.

Because over-imitation reflects sensitivity to norms (Kenward, 2012), we expected parents' higher institutional collectivism to be associated with their children's greater over-imitation of actions likely to trigger normative reasoning.
text.formatted: Because over-imitation reflects sensitivity to norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Kenward, 2012)</ref>, we expected parents' higher institutional collectivism to be associated with their children's greater over-imitation of actions likely to trigger normative reasoning.

text.text: Researchers showing cross-cultural differences in over-imitation in previous studies could only theorise about the reasons responsible for changes in children's behaviour.
However, they did not quantify these differences.

In addition, through their design, they tested only children embedded in a single culture at a time, assuming a culturally homogeneous environment, even though cultural values differ more strongly between individuals than between countries (Fischer & Schwartz, 2011).
text.formatted: In addition, through their design, they tested only children embedded in a single culture at a time, assuming a culturally homogeneous environment, even though cultural values differ more strongly between individuals than between countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fischer & Schwartz, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Many children, however, grow up in societies that are characterised by cultural, linguistic, and ethnic diversity (Fearon, 2003; Gören, 2013).
text.formatted: Many children, however, grow up in societies that are characterised by cultural, linguistic, and ethnic diversity <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fearon, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Gören, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Even in the European Union and the United States, approximately 25% of children are either born outside their country of residence or have foreign-born parents (Federal Interagency Forum on Child and Family Statistics, 2024; Orav, 2023).
text.formatted: Even in the European Union and the United States, approximately 25% of children are either born outside their country of residence or have foreign-born parents <ref type="bibr">(Federal Interagency Forum on Child and Family Statistics, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Orav, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These regions are less culturally diverse than regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and southern Asia (Fearon, 2003; Gören, 2013).
text.formatted: These regions are less culturally diverse than regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and southern Asia <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fearon, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Gören, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, a large portion of children in Western societies grow up with cultural values from multiple cultures.
For these children, cultural diversity is therefore not only a societal backdrop but a characteristic of their home environment.

Yet, measuring parental cultural values and averaging them into a single score masks the degree to which those values diverge (Smith & Bond, 2019) and thus the diversity in cultural values children experience.
text.formatted: Yet, measuring parental cultural values and averaging them into a single score masks the degree to which those values diverge <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Smith & Bond, 2019)</ref> and thus the diversity in cultural values children experience.

text.text: Children raised by parents from different cultural backgrounds may experience differing cultural values between their parents.
For example, how children react to norm violations is related to culture (Gampe & Daum, 2018).
text.formatted: For example, how children react to norm violations is related to culture <ref type="bibr">(Gampe & Daum, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Children from parents with different cultural values, may receive divergent signals about norm violations.
This is relevant to over-imitation, because it can be explained by norm learning (Kenward, 2012).
text.formatted: This is relevant to over-imitation, because it can be explained by norm learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Kenward, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The present study, therefore, quantifies the cultural distance between parents as a direct measure of the diversity to which children are exposed at home.

Language and culture are often deeply intertwined (Yagiz & Izadpanah, 2013), and individuals who speak different languages may also hold distinct cultural perspectives and values (Purpuri et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Language and culture are often deeply intertwined <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Yagiz & Izadpanah, 2013)</ref>, and individuals who speak different languages may also hold distinct cultural perspectives and values <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Purpuri et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In bilingual families (speaking two languages) or bidialectal families (speaking two dialects of the same language), parents often bring different linguistic and cultural backgrounds, which may introduce greater variability in cultural values within the household.

Because bilingual children often grow up in more culturally diverse environments than monolingual children, they may more frequently encounter to differing or even conflicting norms, and therefore judge norm violations as less transgressive (Iannuccilli et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Because bilingual children often grow up in more culturally diverse environments than monolingual children, they may more frequently encounter to differing or even conflicting norms, and therefore judge norm violations as less transgressive <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Iannuccilli et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: If bilingual children grow up in households with more divergent cultural values, they may receive more varied normative signals, potentially making them more flexible in their over-imitation.
Bilingualism also affects other, non-imitative, aspects of children's social learning.

For instance, bilingual children are better at integrating their interaction partners' visual perspective with their utterances to identify the object being referred to (Yow & Markman, 2015), and at interpreting pointing gestures to clarify ambiguous pronouns (Yow, 2015) and resolve conflicting directional cues (Yow & Markman, 2011).
text.formatted: For instance, bilingual children are better at integrating their interaction partners' visual perspective with their utterances to identify the object being referred to <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Yow & Markman, 2015)</ref>, and at interpreting pointing gestures to clarify ambiguous pronouns <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Yow, 2015)</ref> and resolve conflicting directional cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Yow & Markman, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, studying children from bilingual families offers a valuable opportunity to measure specific cultural values associated with changes in over-imitation and to disentangle the potential effects of cultural and language diversity.

In the current study, we explored the effect of parents'foot_0 cultural values, the difference in cultural values between parents (as a proxy for cultural diversity), and language status (monolingual/bilingual/bidialectal) on preschool children's over-imitation in a goal-directed task, adopted from Schleihauf et al. (2018).

(2018)</ref>.

text.text: Children between the ages of 3.5 and 4.5 years observed a live demonstration in which an experimenter used a wooden rod to remove a marble from a puzzle box.
The demonstration included four causally irrelevant actions followed by the action necessary to retrieve the marble.
The unnecessary actions were: clapping (step 1), moving a lever (step 2), tapping the rod in the palm of the hand (step 3), and using the rod to press a button (step 4).

Clapping and tapping (steps 1 and 3) can be classified as noncontact, actions, whereas moving a lever and pressing a button (steps 2 and 4) can be classified as pseudo-instrumental (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020).
text.formatted: Clapping and tapping (steps 1 and 3) can be classified as noncontact, actions, whereas moving a lever and pressing a button (steps 2 and 4) can be classified as pseudo-instrumental <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Children were then given an opportunity to interact with the puzzle box themselves, and we measured whether they imitated unnecessary actions (i.e., their over-imitation).

In addition, parents completed the GLOBE questionnaire (The Globe Foundation, 2006) to assess their cultural values across nine dimensions (power distance, in-group collectivism, gender egalitarianism, uncertainty avoidance, future orientation, institutional collectivism, performance orientation, humane orientation, and assertiveness; see Table 1, and a questionnaire on the child's language exposure.
text.formatted: In addition, parents completed the GLOBE questionnaire <ref type="bibr">(The Globe Foundation, 2006)</ref> to assess their cultural values across nine dimensions (power distance, in-group collectivism, gender egalitarianism, uncertainty avoidance, future orientation, institutional collectivism, performance orientation, humane orientation, and assertiveness; see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, and a questionnaire on the child's language exposure.

text.text: Cultural diversity was operationalised as the Euclidean distance between the two parents' GLOBE scores across all nine dimensions, capturing the overall degree to which their cultural values diverge.
We combined confirmatory and exploratory approaches.

Following the dual-process perspective on over-imitation (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020), we preregistered the prediction that children whose parents endorse greater institutional collectivism are more likely to over-imitate noncontact actions than children whose parents endorse less institutional collectivism.
text.formatted: Following the dual-process perspective on over-imitation <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020)</ref>, we preregistered the prediction that children whose parents endorse greater institutional collectivism are more likely to over-imitate noncontact actions than children whose parents endorse less institutional collectivism.

text.text: Institutional collectivism refers to the degree to which parents believe that organisational or societal institutions should encourage collective action and the distribution of resources (see Table 1 for all definitions of the assessed cultural domains).
text.formatted: Institutional collectivism refers to the degree to which parents believe that organisational or societal institutions should encourage collective action and the distribution of resources (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> for all definitions of the assessed cultural domains).

text.text: We expected to find this effect specifically in noncontact actions because we expected these actions to trigger children's type 2 processing, causing deliberate consideration of whether or not to copy, and thus be affected by children having more normative goals.
In contrast, we preregistered the prediction that blanket copying of pseudo-instrumental actions would not be influenced by parental cultural values.

We acknowledge that prior work suggests pseudo-instrumental actions may also be modulated by contextual and social factors (Legare & Nielsen, 2015; Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020), but because there is insufficient evidence and no theoretical account directly linking the other cultural dimensions to children's over-imitation, we took an exploratory approach to analyse these associations.

text.text: In addition, we explored whether children's language status predicted cultural distance between their parents, to assess whether bilingualism is linked to cultural diversity within the family.

We recruited N = 133 children between the ages of 3.5 and 4.5 years (M age = 4.05 years, SD age = 0.29), 48.9% were girls.

We chose this age range because four-year-olds are old enough to reliably over-imitate, but young enough that the developmental shift from causal to normative motivations is still ongoing (Clay et al., 2018).

text.text: This study was also part of a larger project on children's social cognition that targeted that particular age range.

Children who were assigned a language status were monolingual Swiss German (n = 41, i.e., not more that 10% input in another language), Swiss German bilingual (n = 44, i.e., at least 20% input in Swiss German and one other language, and not more than 10% input in a third language), or bidialectal (n = 40, i.e., at least 20% input in Swiss German and another variety of German and not more than 10% input in another language/language variety) in accordance with Wermelinger et al. (2017).

text.text: The language exposure of the other children (n = 8) did not fulfil the requirements to be assigned a specific language status, and they were excluded from the analyses including language status.

Bilingual children were exposed to the following languages: English (n = 7), French (n = 5), Spanish (n = 4), Italian (n = 4), Hungarian, Russian, Turkish, Croatian, Portuguese, and Serbian (each n = 2), Icelandic, Greek, Swedish, Norwegian, Finnish, Arabic, Albanian, Mandarin, Tamil, Persian, Polish, and Urdu (each n = 1).
Bidialectal children were exposed to the following language varieties: Standard German (n = 38) and Austrian German (n = 2).
Participants were recruited through the research unit's database, which includes of parents who had expressed interest in participating in studies with their children.
Eligible children were healthy, born full-term (gestational age > 37 weeks), had a birth weight above 2500 g, and had no reported diagnoses of developmental disorders, according to parental reports.

text.text: As compensation, each child received a certificate of participation and a small gift (approximately USD 5,-).
Parents provided informed consent for participation.
The local Ethics Committee of the university approved the general procedure, which adhered to the ethical standards of the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments.
Each session was videotaped and coded from the recording.
Children in our sample predominantly came from families with high socio-economic status.

Most participants lived in households with above-average income (Bundesamt fuer Statistik, 2024): 81.2% of parents reported an income higher than the city average, 9.0% reported an income within the average range, and 5.3% reported a below-average income.
4.5% of parents refrained from answering this question.
Parental education levels were also high.
In 79.7% of households, both parents had completed higher education at a university or a university of applied sciences, while in 15.8% of households, one parent held such a degree.
4.5% of children came from households in which parents had completed other types of education, such as vocational training.
We used an over-imitation task based on the puzzle box, which consists of a transparent container (as described in Hoehl et al., 2014; Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2021; Schleihauf et al., 2018).

text.text: Children were presented with a magnetic rod and a transparent Plexiglas container (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: Children were presented with a magnetic rod and a transparent Plexiglas container (see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Inside the container, a transparent tube held steel marbles.
The tube's opening was covered by a lid that could be lifted to allow access to the marbles.
The marbles could be retrieved by inserting the magnetic rod into the tube's front opening.
A black wooden lever was mounted on top of the box, and a black button enclosed in a transparent square was attached to the bottom right of the container.
The transparent design highlighted the irrelevance of certain actions demonstrated during the modelling phase.
We used a cross-sectional between-subjects design.

text.text: The study took place in the lab at the Department of Psychology at the University of Zurich.
The language of testing was Swiss German, the societal language.
The experimenter welcomed the children and their accompanying parent to the lab's playroom, where they informed parents of the study procedure.
The appointment lasted approximately 45 minutes.

After a familiarisation period in the playroom, the experimenter guided the child and their parent to the study room, where the parent was asked to complete questionnaires on their demographic information, the child's language exposure, the child's Theory of Mind (irrelevant to the current study), and their own cultural values on a tablet.
As previously mentioned, this study was part of a bigger project.

Thus, the procedure started with a task measuring receptive vocabulary (BILEX; Gampe et al., 2018), followed by visual perspective-taking (Director's task; Agostini et al., 2024), and non-verbal cue understanding (Yow & Markman, 2011), which were counterbalanced in order.
text.formatted: Thus, the procedure started with a task measuring receptive vocabulary (BILEX; <ref type="bibr">Gampe et al., 2018)</ref>, followed by visual perspective-taking (Director's task; <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Agostini et al., 2024)</ref>, and non-verbal cue understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Yow & Markman, 2011)</ref>, which were counterbalanced in order.

text.text: Then, the over-imitation task was administered.
The tasks administered after the over-imitation task assessed inhibition and task-switching.
If children were bilingual or bidialectal, they participated in a receptive vocabulary task in their other language at the end of the procedure.
The over-imitation task was administered approximately midway through the procedure, so that the children were more familiar with the experimenter but not yet fatigued.
The experimenter followed the same task procedure for each child.
The full procedure was recorded on video and coded afterwards.
Upon completing each task in the procedure, the child earned a sticker for a sticker-collection card they received at the start of the appointment.
The procedure of the over-imitation task is an adaptation from Schleihauf et al. (2018) and consists of only the "Transparent Tube Condition".
text.formatted: The procedure of the over-imitation task is an adaptation from <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Schleihauf et al. (2018)</ref> and consists of only the "Transparent Tube Condition".

text.text: It involves a modelling phase and a testing phase, and it does not include any manipulation of experimenter characteristics.
Modelling Phase.
The experimenter placed the transparent container on a table in front of the child, but angled towards herself, and took a seat on a chair next to the child.
She asked the child to pay close attention, then performed a series of four redundant actions, before lifting the lid and obtaining the marble with the magnetic rod.
The order of the action was standardised and the same across participants.

The experimenter 1) clapped her hands three times, 2) pushed the lever from left to right and back, 3) tapped the magnetic rod in her left hand three times, and 4) used the back of the magnetic rod to push the black button.

As classified by Schleihauf and Hoehl (2020), two of these actions were noncontact (steps 1 and 3; clapping and tapping), and two were pseudo-instrumental (steps 2 and 4; pushing the lever and the button).
text.formatted: As classified by <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Schleihauf and Hoehl (2020)</ref>, two of these actions were noncontact (steps 1 and 3; clapping and tapping), and two were pseudo-instrumental (steps 2 and 4; pushing the lever and the button).

text.text: The experimenter then opened the lid, inserted the magnetic tip into the tube to retrieve the marble, and showed it to the child.
Testing Phase.
After the modelling phase, the experimenter turned the transparent container towards the child and said: "Now it's your turn.
You can do it however you want.
You can't go wrong."
(Swiss German: "Jetzt bisch du dra.
Du chaschs eso mache, wie du möchtisch.
Du chasch nüt falsch mache").
While the child interacted with the transparent container, the experimenter went to organise a cupboard, so as not to pressure the child by observing them.
The experimenter turned around, towards the cupboard, her back and side towards the child, but did not leave the room.
The child was therefore outside her field of view, and they could not see the experimenter's face.
The over-imitation phase ended when the child signalled to the experimenter that they had got a marble out and confirmed that they were finished playing with the puzzle box.
The full procedure was recorded on video.
