text.text: Children's over-imitation was measured using the over-imitation task (see Procedure).
A trained observer coded the over-imitation of each redundant action from video.
They coded whether the child performed or attempted to perform (e.g., clapping once instead of three times) the action during the testing phase (as "1") or not (as "0") in a spreadsheet.
A second trained observer coded the videos from 30 children (23% of the sample) using the same procedure.
We computed inter-observer reliability using Cohen's Kappa for binary categories (action imitated vs. not).
The kappa value was 0.93, indicating almost perfect (96.7%) agreement between coders (Landis & Koch, 1977).
text.formatted: The kappa value was 0.93, indicating almost perfect (96.7%) agreement between coders <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Landis & Koch, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: In case of disagreements between the observers, we used the values from the first observer, who coded the entire dataset.

We differentiated between noncontact actions (actions that do not involve physical interaction with the transparent container, i.e., actions 1 and 3) and pseudo-instrumental actions (actions that do involve physical contact with the container, i.e., actions 2 and 4).
Children's language status was measured using the Language Exposure questionnaire for Multilinguals Online (LEMON; https://www.quassel.ch/; Openscript GmbH, 2025).
text.formatted: Children's language status was measured using the Language Exposure questionnaire for Multilinguals Online (LEMON; <ref type="url" target="https://www.quassel.ch/">https://www.quassel.ch/</ref>; Openscript GmbH, 2025).

text.text: Parents were asked for the amount of time the child spends with each interaction partner and is exposed to each language/language variety for each caregiving situation since the child's birthday, for each day of the week, each interaction partner, and each language.
We determined language status based on the amount of time the child is exposed to each language/language variety.
All children in our sample were exposed to the societal language, Swiss German.

Parental cultural values were assessed using a digitalised version of the Global Leadership and Organizational Behaviour Effectiveness (GLOBE; House et al., 2004) survey, openly available through https://globeproject.com/data/GLOBE-Phase-2-Beta-Questionnaire-2006.pdf.
text.formatted: Parental cultural values were assessed using a digitalised version of the Global Leadership and Organizational Behaviour Effectiveness (GLOBE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">House et al., 2004)</ref> survey, openly available through <ref type="url" target="https://globeproject.com/data/GLOBE-Phase-2-Beta-Questionnaire-2006.pdf">https://globeproject.com/data/GLOBE-Phase-2-Beta-Questionnaire-2006.pdf</ref>.

text.text: The parent accompanying the child during the lab appointment completed the questionnaire during this visit.
The questionnaire was subsequently sent to the other parent (if applicable) by email.

The GLOBE consists of nine cultural dimensions: power orientation, in-group collectivism, gender egalitarianism, uncertainty avoidance, future orientation, institutional collectivism, performance orientation, humane orientation, and assertiveness.
The scales describe "between-society" differences, see Table 1 for definitions of the cultural dimensions and S6 in the supplementary materials for the internal consistency on the dimensions.
text.formatted: The scales describe "between-society" differences, see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> for definitions of the cultural dimensions and S6 in the supplementary materials for the internal consistency on the dimensions.

text.text: [Insert Table 1 here] The questionnaire distinguishes between how the respondent perceives the society they reside in ("as is") versus how they believe a society should aspire to be ("should be").
text.formatted: [Insert Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> here] The questionnaire distinguishes between how the respondent perceives the society they reside in ("as is") versus how they believe a society should aspire to be ("should be").

text.text: The current study included only the "should be" values because all participants lived within the same society and therefore shared a common social context, making differences in parents' perceived cultural practices unlikely to be a major source of between-participant variance.

In contrast, there is substantial individual variation in values about how a society should function, and perceptions of current social practices may not reflect the personal ideals that parents aspire to (Fischer & Boer, 2016; Fischer & Schwartz, 2011)."
text.formatted: In contrast, there is substantial individual variation in values about how a society should function, and perceptions of current social practices may not reflect the personal ideals that parents aspire to <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Fischer & Boer, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Fischer & Schwartz, 2011)</ref>."

text.text: Should be" values, therefore, capture the cultural values children are exposed to through their parents more directly than parents' perceptions of the current societal norms.
The subscale consists of 39 questions on a 7-point Likert scale.
The final score is calculated as the mean score of both parents.
To assess differences between parents' values, we calculated a Euclidean distance score (Carlier et al., 2024) based on their responses to the GLOBE questionnaire (House et al., 2004).
text.formatted: To assess differences between parents' values, we calculated a Euclidean distance score <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Carlier et al., 2024)</ref> based on their responses to the GLOBE questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(House et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Euclidean distance is widely used in multidimensional scaling and psychological research (Carlier et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Euclidean distance is widely used in multidimensional scaling and psychological research <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Carlier et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: It aggregates discrepancies across multiple dimensions into a single continuous measure, giving greater weight to larger differences and capturing overall multidimensional divergence.

For each cultural dimension, we first computed the difference between the two parents' scores and combined them into a single measure reflecting the overall discrepancy between parents' cultural values (D):
With n as the total number of assessed cultural dimensions, i as the answered cultural dimension, and x and y for the cultural values of parents 1 and 2 on this dimension.
Our preregistered models included each different dimension of parental cultural values (analysed separately), age, action type and action step.

Because the different steps were the same for all children (steps 1 and 3 were noncontact, and steps 2 and 4 were pseudo-instrumental), action type and action step in the model were collinear, which caused convergence problems.
We, therefore, removed action type to obtain stable models and examined its effect through post-hoc contrasts computed on the posterior draws.
Specifically, we compared the average estimate for steps 1 and 3 with the average estimate for steps 2 and 4.
Because action step was sum-coded, the coefficient for step 4 was reconstructed as the negative sum of the coefficients for steps 1, 2, and 3.
The planned contrast was therefore calculated as: ((step 1 + step 3) -(step 2 + step 4)) / 2.
This contrast was computed for both the main effect of action step and the interaction between action step and the predictor of interest.
The interaction contrast tested whether the association between the predictor and over-imitation differed between these two groups of action steps.
For full model parameters, see Table S1 in supplementary materials.
text.formatted: For full model parameters, see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref> in supplementary materials.

text.text: It should be noted that action step and action type are not equivalent.
Whilst they were collinear, action step additionally captures variance that may be attributed to presentation order and working memory demands.
The post-hoc contrasts for action type should therefore be interpreted with caution, as step-related factors cannot be fully disentangled from action-type effects.
We analysed our data using Bayesian Generalised Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs).
Because the outcome variable was binary (the action was either imitated or not), we modelled it with a Bernoulli distribution.
We used random intercepts for each child to account for repeated measurements across action steps.
The nine models on parental cultural values had the following structure: over-imitation ∼ score on dimension of parental cultural values * action step (4 levels) + age + (1|child).

We analysed the effect of cultural diversity with the following model: over-imitation ∼ cultural diversity * action step (4 levels) + age + (1|child), and the effect of language status with the following model: over-imitation ∼ language status (3 levels) * action step (4 levels) + age + (1|child).
All models were fitted using the brms package (Bürkner, 2017) in R (R Core Team, 2025).
text.formatted: All models were fitted using the brms package <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bürkner, 2017)</ref> in R (R Core Team, 2025).

text.text: We standardised all predictors to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
We contrast-coded all categorical predictors to sum up to a mean of 1.
We used weakly informative priors for the fixed effects of interest being norm(0, 1), norm(0, 10) for age, and the default norm prior provided by the brms package (Bürkner, 2017) for action step.
text.formatted: We used weakly informative priors for the fixed effects of interest being norm(0, 1), norm(0, 10) for age, and the default norm prior provided by the brms package <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bürkner, 2017)</ref> for action step.

text.text: We used probability of direction (pd) as our reference index (Makowski et al., 2019) for the fixed effects and accepted our hypothesis if the pd >= 90%.

Further, we excluded another 8 children from the analyses containing language status, because they did not fulfil the inclusion criterion regarding language exposure.
From the analyses containing cultural diversity, we excluded 23 children, because the GLOBE questionnaire was completed by only one parent, and cultural diversity could therefore not be calculated.

text.text: Further, we analysed whether a family's language status predicted the difference in cultural values between parents.
We did not find evidence of an association between language status and cultural differences (pd < 90%).
text.formatted: We did not find evidence of an association between language status and cultural differences (pd < 90%).

text.text: To check whether our measure of cultural diversity was sensitive enough to detect the different variability between couples, we conducted a non-preregistered analysis in which we compared the Euclidean distances within couples to those calculated between any pair of parents.

The model showed that the Euclidean distance in couples was smaller than in any random pair (Median β = 0.21, 89%CI[0.08, 0.35], pd = 99.60%), meaning that couples show smaller differences in their cultural values than randomly compared individuals.

This study investigated the relationship between parental cultural values, the difference between them (as a proxy for cultural diversity), language status, and children's over-imitation of redundant pseudo-instrumental and noncontact actions.
We recruited 3.5 to 4.5-year-olds from a wider Zurich area.
The sample came from families with a predominantly high SES.
Children observed an adult experimenter performing redundant actions on a transparent puzzle box before removing a marble from it.
They were then given the opportunity to interact with the puzzle box themselves.
Overall, children over-imitated pseudo-instrumental actions more often than noncontact actions.
This is in line with previous findings (Clay et al., 2018) and the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020).
text.formatted: This is in line with previous findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clay et al., 2018)</ref> and the dual-process perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Language status was not associated with children's over-imitation.
Parental institutional collectivism was negatively associated with children's over-imitation, regardless of action type.

The pattern of relationships between parental cultural values on several other dimensions was complex, with some dimensions showing a main effect (e.g., performance orientation), and others interacting with action type (e.g., in-group collectivism or power distance).
The distance between parental cultural values across all dimensions, used as a proxy for cultural diversity in children's environment, also interacted with the action type.
Pseudo-instrumental, but not noncontact actions, were less likely to be imitated by children whose parents differed more in their cultural values.
These relationships could not be explained by children's language status, because parental cultural values did not differ between monolingual, bilingual and bidialectal children.
To sum up, parental cultural values, but not children's language status, influenced children's over-imitation of redundant actions.
Contrary to our hypothesis, parental institutional collectivism was negatively associated with over-imitation, regardless of action type.
This suggests that children of parents with stronger institutional collectivist values were less likely to reproduce redundant actions overall.
As defined above, these two dimensions operate at different levels of social organisation.
Institutional collectivism concerns societal-level collective action, whereas in-group collectivism reflects loyalty and cohesion within families and social groups.

In line with the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020), we expected cultural dimensions would be associated with children's over-imitation of noncontact, but not pseudo-instrumental, actions, because these actions trigger deliberate considerations of whether or not to copy.
text.formatted: In line with the dual-process perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020)</ref>, we expected cultural dimensions would be associated with children's over-imitation of noncontact, but not pseudo-instrumental, actions, because these actions trigger deliberate considerations of whether or not to copy.

text.text: We based our predictions for the dimension of institutional collectivism on the work of Gampe and Daum (2018).
text.formatted: We based our predictions for the dimension of institutional collectivism on the work of <ref type="bibr">Gampe and Daum (2018)</ref>.

text.text: They found that bicultural children of parents with higher values of institutional collectivism intervened less saliently (more implicitly) when responding to norm violations.
The authors suggested that higher institutional collectivism implies stronger group loyalty and less enforcement of norms on an individual level.

Accordingly, we hypothesised that higher degrees of group loyalty would lead to higher levels of over-imitation of noncontact actions because children would apply the perceived norms by imitating them.

One possible explanation is that institutional collectivistic values guide parents' behaviour at a broader, systemic level, (e.g., "I believe that the economic system in this society should be designed to maximize (individual interests: 1; collective interests; 7)";
The Globe Foundation, 2006, p.15) and may therefore have a weaker impact on children's everyday social interactions.

By contrast, in-group collectivistic values may shape caregiving styles (e.g., "Members of this society should (take no pride in being a member of the society: 1; take a great deal of pride in being a member of the society: 7)"; The Globe Foundation, 2006, p.18) and expectations for children's social behaviour (Gorla et al., 2024).
text.formatted: By contrast, in-group collectivistic values may shape caregiving styles (e.g., "Members of this society should (take no pride in being a member of the society: 1; take a great deal of pride in being a member of the society: <ref type="formula">7</ref>)"; The Globe Foundation, 2006, p.18) and expectations for children's social behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gorla et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These values may shape children's behaviour more directly toward conformity and affiliation and, consequently, could explain their greater imitation of redundant actions if they interpreted them as normative (Clegg & Legare, 2016).
text.formatted: These values may shape children's behaviour more directly toward conformity and affiliation and, consequently, could explain their greater imitation of redundant actions if they interpreted them as normative <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clegg & Legare, 2016</ref>).

text.text: An alternative explanation concerns norm salience, rather than norm adherence.

The link between higher institutional collectivism and less explicit responses to norm violations (Gampe & Daum, 2018) could reflect reduced individual-level norm enforcement, rather than stronger group loyalty.
text.formatted: The link between higher institutional collectivism and less explicit responses to norm violations <ref type="bibr">(Gampe & Daum, 2018)</ref> could reflect reduced individual-level norm enforcement, rather than stronger group loyalty.

text.text: Children from higher institutional collectivism backgrounds may perceive norm enforcement as a collective or institutional responsibility, rather than a personal one.
This may lead them to feel less compelled to over-imitate overtly.
In this case, lower over-imitation would reflect reduced individual norm salience rather than weaker normative motivations.
Exploratory analyses showed different patterns of associations between other dimensions of parental cultural values and children's over-imitation.

Parental gender egalitarianism, assertiveness, power distance, and performance orientation were associated with children's over-imitation patterns, and showed both differences in imitation across action types and overall levels of over-imitation.
The cultural dimensions humane orientation, future orientation, and uncertainty avoidance showed no associations with children's over-imitation.
Because of the exploratory nature of these analyses, the results should be interpreted with caution, and any explanation for these associations is speculative.

Although exploratory, these findings are consistent with the previous findings showing the extent to which children over-imitate differs between cultures (Berl & Hewlett, 2015; Clegg & Legare, 2016; Fong et al., 2021; Nielsen & Tomaselli, 2010; Nielsen et al., 2014; Stengelin et al., 2019 Stengelin et al., , 2020)).
text.formatted: Although exploratory, these findings are consistent with the previous findings showing the extent to which children over-imitate differs between cultures <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Berl & Hewlett, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Clegg & Legare, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Fong et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Nielsen & Tomaselli, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Nielsen et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Stengelin et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Stengelin et al., , 2020))</ref>.

text.text: Here, we recruited children living in the wider Zurich area in Switzerland, and we directly quantified the cultural values in children's environments that might have produced these differences, whereas previous research relied on contrasts between specific nations.
Parents have an important impact on children's cultural values, but so do the cultural norms within the society where children are raised (Kalmijn, 2015).
text.formatted: Parents have an important impact on children's cultural values, but so do the cultural norms within the society where children are raised <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Kalmijn, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: We did not measure prevalent societal values or how far the parents in our study deviated from or adhered to them, so we could not capture the entirety of the cultural environment of the children.

To sum up, parental in-group collectivism was positively associated with the over-imitation of both types of actions, possibly showing increased norm adherence in children of parents who endorse group loyalty and mutual dependence within families and social groups.
However, the overall association between parental cultural values and their children's over-imitation varies per dimension of cultural values, which makes drawing general conclusions difficult.
Further research could explore the full impact of children's cultural environment by examining both parental and societal values, the distance between them and their impact on over-imitation.

In addition to specific cultural dimensions influencing children's over-imitation, we found that the distance between parents' cultural values across the nine value dimensions was associated with children's over-imitation of pseudo-instrumental actions only.

Children whose parents had low differences in cultural values over-imitated pseudo-instrumental actions more than children whose parents had high differences, but their over-imitation of noncontact actions was comparable.
Children who grow up in homes with divergent cultural values may encounter more normative ambiguity in daily life.
This may increase their sensitivity to behaviours with unclear causal function, which in turn may prompt deliberate consideration of whether or not to copy (type 2 processing).
Pseudo-instrumental actions could be particularly subject to this, as their causal irrelevance is less clear than for noncontact actions.
Bicultural households show greater flexibility in norm-related judgments (Iannuccilli et al., 2021) and develop more nuanced strategies for interpreting ambiguous social information (Kalmijn, 2015).
text.formatted: Bicultural households show greater flexibility in norm-related judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Iannuccilli et al., 2021)</ref> and develop more nuanced strategies for interpreting ambiguous social information <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Kalmijn, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Children from culturally diverse households may therefore be more used to causal ambiguity, which pseudo-instrumental actions can cause.
This contrasts with the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020), which predicts blanket copying rather than deliberate consideration for pseudo-instrumental actions.
text.formatted: This contrasts with the dual-process perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020)</ref>, which predicts blanket copying rather than deliberate consideration for pseudo-instrumental actions.

text.text: However, all explanations are speculative, given the exploratory nature of this analysis, but they present a promising avenue for future research.
Quantifying the cultural diversity children grow up in is worthwhile, as it captures a source of diversity in children's environments that remains masked when averaging the scores across parents.
Moreover, children may have parents with identical mean cultural scores, yet have fundamentally different experiences in their home environments.
This ranges from growing up with parents with the same cultural backgrounds to parents with completely opposite cultural values.
Parental cultural values, however, are only one of the influential components in children's cultural environments.
Children receive cultural input from caregivers beyond their parents or primary caregivers, such as peers (Rogoff, 1981) or teachers in educational settings (Scheidecker et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Children receive cultural input from caregivers beyond their parents or primary caregivers, such as peers <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Rogoff, 1981)</ref> or teachers in educational settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Scheidecker et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Childcare teachers, for example, carry cultural beliefs about developmental goals and collaboration affecting their teaching practices (van Schaik et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Childcare teachers, for example, carry cultural beliefs about developmental goals and collaboration affecting their teaching practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(van Schaik et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: This is relevant, given that most cross-cultural research assumes homogeneous environments (Smith & Bond, 2019), which overlooks the diversity that children experience in their everyday lives (Padilla, 2008; Yulianto, 2023).
text.formatted: This is relevant, given that most cross-cultural research assumes homogeneous environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Smith & Bond, 2019)</ref>, which overlooks the diversity that children experience in their everyday lives <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Padilla, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Yulianto, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, capturing the cultural values of everyone in children's lives presents a methodological challenge.
The current study's contribution of capturing the cultural values of both caregivers, and quantifying the distance between them, is a first step in that direction.
One possible explanation for our findings is that, in the present age group, pseudo-instrumental actions may be more likely to trigger type 2 processing than the non-contact actions.

Because the children in our sample were of preschool age and younger than those in most previous studies (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020), they may not have fully developed the blanket copying heuristic yet (McGuigan & Whiten, 2009), and relied on type 2 processing instead.

text.text: Evidence suggests that infants already show deliberate consideration of whether to copy others' actions (Gergely & Csibra, 2003; Gergely et al., 2002), but see also Beisert et al. (2012) and Paulus et al. (2011) for alternative explanations.

(2012)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Paulus et al. (2011)</ref> for alternative explanations.

text.text: If blanket copying has not been fully developed, neither action type should then elicit type 1 processing.
This would mean that both types of actions elicit type 2 processing, triggering deliberate considerations on whether or not to copy.
In turn, factors such as culture (Clegg & Legare, 2016; Fong et al., 2021) or social or normative goals (Hoehl et al., 2019) could influence this.

text.text: In addition, children's perception of causal relevance to object-bound actions could explain that preschool children copy object-focused (pseudo-instrumental) actions more than older children (Clay et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In addition, children's perception of causal relevance to object-bound actions could explain that preschool children copy object-focused (pseudo-instrumental) actions more than older children <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clay et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: With age, children's focus shifts from their assumptions about causality to social (Nielsen & Blank, 2011) and normative (Kenward, 2012) context of the demonstration.

text.text: As the current sample consisted of children between 3.5 to 4.5 years of age, children were likely to consider copying actions based on their possible causal relevance.
This account, however, does not explain why the two action types showed different patterns of association with cultural variables.
If both elicit type 2 processing, both should be susceptible to cultural influence, yet this was not what we observed.

We used a transparent puzzle box, which could have made the children realise that the pseudo-instrumental actions were not causally relevant (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020; Schleihauf et al., 2018), thereby making it more likely that type 2 processing would be triggered.
text.formatted: We used a transparent puzzle box, which could have made the children realise that the pseudo-instrumental actions were not causally relevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Schleihauf et al., 2018)</ref>, thereby making it more likely that type 2 processing would be triggered.

text.text: Furthermore, the social context of the task may have shaped children's motivation for imitation because imitation serves both instrumental and social communicative functions (Over & Carpenter, 2013; Uzgiris, 1981).
text.formatted: Furthermore, the social context of the task may have shaped children's motivation for imitation because imitation serves both instrumental and social communicative functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Over & Carpenter, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Uzgiris, 1981)</ref>.

text.text: Besides learning about an object, children may copy behaviour to communicate social alignment.

In this study's procedure, however, after demonstrating the action sequence, the experimenter disengaged from the child and turned to another activity, while the child interacted with the puzzle box to retrieve the marble.
This design choice may have reduced the child's social-communicative motivation, as they did not interact with the experimenter during the puzzle box task.
Children's copying behaviour may, therefore, have been primarily driven by instrumental rather than affiliative goals.
As a result, children may have disregarded noncontact actions that were clearly redundant immediately.
In contrast, pseudo-instrumental actions may have elicited deliberate consideration, which showed association with parents' cultural values and the cultural diversity in the home environment.
Because of children's focus on the object and the nature of the task, we suggest that type 2 processing could have been elicited for the pseudo-instrumental actions.

Working memory may have modulated this process as well, given that actions demonstrated later (steps 3 and 4) were more likely to be reproduced than those demonstrated earlier (steps 1 and 2), for both noncontact and pseudo-instrumental actions.

This suggests that the retention and deliberate consideration of whether or not to copy actions could depend partly on children's working memory capacity as well (Rusnak et al., 2022; Speidel et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This suggests that the retention and deliberate consideration of whether or not to copy actions could depend partly on children's working memory capacity as well <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Rusnak et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Speidel et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Because we did not measure working memory in this study, this remains speculative.

Individual differences in parents' cultural values and the cultural diversity of the home environment may, therefore, be more likely to shape children's imitation patterns of pseudo-instrumental actions or all actions equally, a pattern we found for several individual dimensions of parental cultural values as well.
The present findings suggest that the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020) could be refined to solve the tension noted above.
text.formatted: The present findings suggest that the dual-process perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020)</ref> could be refined to solve the tension noted above.

text.text: Rather than assuming both action types elicit type 2 processing, responses to causally irrelevant actions may vary along a continuum depending on how readily their irrelevance can be detected.
The current framework distinguishes between type 1 blanket copying, triggered by causally ambiguous actions, and type 2 deliberate considerations, triggered when causal irrelevance is recognised.
The present results, however, suggest that causally irrelevant actions could be conceptualised along a continuum, depending on how readily the causal irrelevance can be detected.

When causal irrelevance is highly salient (i.e., with noncontact actions), children may dismiss the action automatically, without deliberation, resulting in low copying, regardless of cultural or contextual factors (blanket non-copying), similar to type 1 processing but in the opposite direction.

When causal irrelevance is moderately ambiguous (i.e., with pseudo-instrumental actions), children may deliberately consider whether or not to copy, which could be influenced by cultural and contextual factors.
When causal irrelevance is very hard to detect, children may blankly copy.
In addition, how easy it is to detect the causal irrelevance could also vary with age, consistent with previous findings (Clay et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In addition, how easy it is to detect the causal irrelevance could also vary with age, consistent with previous findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clay et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Such a continuum represents the current findings more cleanly than the proposed dual-process framework and could guide future research into the conditions under which each mode of processing is activated.
The association between parental cultural values and children's over-imitation is consistent with a normative account of the dual-process Perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020).
text.formatted: The association between parental cultural values and children's over-imitation is consistent with a normative account of the dual-process Perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Higher parental in-group collectivism was associated with greater over-imitation, suggesting that children of parents who endorse group loyalty and mutual dependence within families or social groups may have stronger normative motivations to copy the demonstrated actions.

The aligns with previous cross-cultural findings showing that children from more collectivistic backgrounds over-imitate more, which is attributed to greater norm-conformity (Clegg & Legare, 2016; Fong et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The aligns with previous cross-cultural findings showing that children from more collectivistic backgrounds over-imitate more, which is attributed to greater norm-conformity <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clegg & Legare, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Fong et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, normative processes may not be the only mechanism through which culture shapes over-imitation.
Cultural values may equally affect children's instrumental or affiliative goals (Hoehl et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Cultural values may equally affect children's instrumental or affiliative goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hoehl et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Children from certain cultural backgrounds may be more motivated to learn from demonstrated actions for instrumental reasons, or may copy actions to signal social alignment with the experimenter.
These processes could also contribute to the pattern of associations we observed between parental cultural values and children's over-imitation we observed.

Neither a purely normative nor a purely instrumental or affiliative account fully explains why the influence of parental cultural values and cultural diversity was stronger for pseudo-instrumental than noncontact actions, contrary to the predictions of the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020).
text.formatted: Neither a purely normative nor a purely instrumental or affiliative account fully explains why the influence of parental cultural values and cultural diversity was stronger for pseudo-instrumental than noncontact actions, contrary to the predictions of the dual-process perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Disentangling these mechanisms would require study designs that explicitly manipulate the framing of the task by, for example, presenting actions as either normative or instrumental (Clay et al., 2018; Keupp et al., 2013) or by introducing conditions on the experimenter's presence during the testing phase (Nielsen & Blank, 2011).
text.formatted: Disentangling these mechanisms would require study designs that explicitly manipulate the framing of the task by, for example, presenting actions as either normative or instrumental <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clay et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Keupp et al., 2013)</ref> or by introducing conditions on the experimenter's presence during the testing phase <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Nielsen & Blank, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: If children's cultural environments shape their over-imitation through normative motivations, effects should become apparent in normative framings and when the experimenter is present.
If cultural environments shape children's over-imitation through cognitive processes, no differences should be observed between the framings or in absence or presence of the experimenter.
One unexplored avenue in this line of research is the possibility that culture can affect children's over-imitation by influencing their cognition.

A large body of previous research (e.g., Chiao, 2018; Kuwabara & Smith, 2012; Saxe & de Kirby, 2014) explains how culture can affect children's cognitive development, for instance, what they attend to during an event and what they learn from it (Qi & Roberts, 2019), and their socio-cognitive development (Kärtner et al., 2020).
text.formatted: A large body of previous research (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Chiao, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Kuwabara & Smith, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Saxe & de Kirby, 2014)</ref> explains how culture can affect children's cognitive development, for instance, what they attend to during an event and what they learn from it <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Qi & Roberts, 2019)</ref>, and their socio-cognitive development <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Kärtner et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Based on our findings, future research should examine which mechanisms, normative or cognitive, are behind the effects of children's cultural environment on their over-imitation.
For instance, by framing all actions as either normative or instrumental (Clay et al., 2018; Keupp et al., 2013) or having the researcher present or absent (Nielsen & Blank, 2011).
text.formatted: For instance, by framing all actions as either normative or instrumental <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clay et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Keupp et al., 2013)</ref> or having the researcher present or absent <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Nielsen & Blank, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: If children's cultural environment affects their over-imitation through its impact on children's normative motivations, it should affect children's behaviour in the normative, but not instrumental framing, and in the presence of the researcher.

If it affects children's over-imitation by influencing their cognitive processes when they observe the action demonstration, then the framing or presence of the researcher should have no influence on their behaviour.

The results from such research could be used to further expand the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020) and other theoretical perspectives on over-imitation to encompass the full range of cultural effects.
text.formatted: The results from such research could be used to further expand the dual-process perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020</ref>) and other theoretical perspectives on over-imitation to encompass the full range of cultural effects.

text.text: Growing up with more than one culture often comes with learning more than one language.
Here, we did not find evidence that children's language status (i.e., being monolingual, bilingual, or bidialectal) affected their over-imitation, regardless of the action type.
All children over-imitated both action types at similar levels.
The fact that parents of bilingual or bidialectal children did not exhibit larger differences in cultural values than parents of monolingual children might explain this finding.

As we could still show that partners have more cultural values in common than randomly paired people, it is unlikely that low sensitivity of our cultural diversity measures causes this pattern of results.
Therefore, parents in our study had largely homogeneous cultural values, despite, at least for some of them, coming from different cultural backgrounds.

Because we did not collect data on the parents' country of origin, some parents may have been either second-or third-generation immigrants (and thus assimilated into Swiss culture), or are from a different part of the country, e.g., French-or Italian-speaking.
Therefore, bilingual children in our study (and in the general population in Switzerland) can, but do not have to be, bicultural as well.
This highlights the need to measure children's cultural environment when investigating the effects of bilingualism on children's social behaviour.

Bilinguals are a very heterogeneous group (Wermelinger et al., 2024), and without the measurement of the different sources of variability in their environment, the results of one study finding a difference between monolinguals and bilinguals might not generalise to other bilingual populations (Byers-Heinlein et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Bilinguals are a very heterogeneous group <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Wermelinger et al., 2024)</ref>, and without the measurement of the different sources of variability in their environment, the results of one study finding a difference between monolinguals and bilinguals might not generalise to other bilingual populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Byers-Heinlein et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The current study offers several strengths by exploring different factors that explain children's over-imitation behaviour, building on and expanding the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020).

text.text: However, some methodological limitations should be noted.

First, the use of the GLOBE questionnaire (House et al., 2004) to assess parents' cultural values imposes conceptual constraints, as the questionnaire was originally developed to assess culture and value orientations in leadership and workplace contexts, rather than at the level of individual parents or family interactions (House et al., 2004 (House et al., , 2014)).
text.formatted: First, the use of the GLOBE questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(House et al., 2004)</ref> to assess parents' cultural values imposes conceptual constraints, as the questionnaire was originally developed to assess culture and value orientations in leadership and workplace contexts, rather than at the level of individual parents or family interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(House et al., 2004</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(House et al., , 2014))</ref>.

text.text: Although GLOBE measures have been adapted for use with individuals (Gampe & Daum, 2018; Gorla et al., 2024), the connection between the GLOBE dimensions and individual-level caregiving practices remains unknown.
text.formatted: Although GLOBE measures have been adapted for use with individuals <ref type="bibr">(Gampe & Daum, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Gorla et al., 2024)</ref>, the connection between the GLOBE dimensions and individual-level caregiving practices remains unknown.

text.text: As a result, the present analyses are exploratory, and the findings should be interpreted as identifying associations rather than providing evidence for causal relationships.
The current results highlight the need for future research into different dimensions of culture, parents' cultural values, and ways to measure these at the family-level in caregiving contexts.

Second, it is worth noting that GLOBE's definition of in-group collectivism emphasises loyalty and group pride relevant in the context of leadership and workplace contexts, which is different from how collectivism in conceptualised in the broader literature, which focuses more strongly on interdependence, social obligation, and conformity (Hofstede, 2001; Triandis, 2018).
text.formatted: Second, it is worth noting that GLOBE's definition of in-group collectivism emphasises loyalty and group pride relevant in the context of leadership and workplace contexts, which is different from how collectivism in conceptualised in the broader literature, which focuses more strongly on interdependence, social obligation, and conformity <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Hofstede, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Triandis, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, the experimental design minimised normative and social cues during both Modelling and Testing phases.
After demonstrating the action sequence, the experimenter disengaged while the child interacted with the puzzle box.

While this approach allowed for the assessment of children's spontaneous copying of redundant actions, it may have reduced social pressure and communicative motivation for imitation (Kenward et al., 2011; Legare & Nielsen, 2015; Over & Carpenter, 2013).

text.text: This methodological decision may have shifted children's focus toward instrumental interpretations of actions rather than to social affiliation or norm adherence (Legare et al., 2015).

text.text: As noted above, actions presented later were more likely to be reproduced (steps 3 and 4 vs. steps 1 and 2), consistent with a memory account and suggesting that step-related variance is real and non-trivial (see ??).
Future studies should counterbalance the order of noncontact and pseudo-instrumental actions to disentangle these effects cleanly.

Although these methodological constraints in this study prevented us from exploring the mechanisms underlying the influence of parental cultural values on children's over-imitation, the findings open a new research avenue.

The present study indicates that how preschool children over-imitate is associated with parental cultural values. 4-year-old children over-imitated pseudo-instrumental actions more than noncontact actions, highlighting their object-directed orientation at this developmental stage.
The pattern of associations of several dimensions of parental cultural values to children's over-imitation was complex.

Contrary to the predictions of the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020), children's cultural environment was associated with their over-imitation of pseudo-instrumental actions more than noncontact actions.
text.formatted: Contrary to the predictions of the dual-process perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020</ref>), children's cultural environment was associated with their over-imitation of pseudo-instrumental actions more than noncontact actions.

text.text: These results suggest that preschool children do not yet apply blanket copying to pseudo-instrumental actions, or that culture has an effect above and beyond children's normative motivation to over-imitate, and rather shapes how they process and learn from social interactions.

Rather than a binary distinction between blanket copying and deliberate consideration, responses to causally irrelevant actions may vary along a continuum of how readily the irrelevance can be detected.

Highly salient irrelevance may produce blanket non-copying, moderate ambiguity may trigger deliberate consideration, which could be influenced by cultural factors, and low salience of irrelevance may produce blanket copying.

Overall, this study suggests that children's over-imitation is shaped not only by the properties of the demonstrated actions but also by the children's cultural environments, highlighting the importance of integrating individual cultural contexts into theories on social learning. review and editing.

The current study focuses on the individual factors that might influence children's over-imitation, specifically children's cultural background.
Figure 4.
Parental assertiveness interacted with action type (Median β = -0.49, 89%CI[-0.90, -0.07], pd = 97.17%).
Higher assertiveness was associated with children's increased imitation of pseudo-instrumental actions, but not of noncontact actions.
Similarly, parental gender egalitarianism interacted with action type (Median β = 0.55, 89%CI[0.13, 0.96], pd = 98.45%).
Children of parents reporting lower gender egalitarianism imitated more pseudo-instrumental than noncontact actions.
In contrast, children of parents reporting higher gender egalitarianism imitated both action types equally.
Parental performance orientation showed a main effect on over-imitation (Median β = 0.22, 89%CI[-0.05, 0.51], pd = 90.65%).
Higher parental performance orientation was associated to a greater likelihood of children imitating the observed actions, regardless of action type.

Parental in-group collectivism was positively associated with over-imitation (Median β = 0.27, 89%CI[-0.02, 0.58], pd = 93.03%), predicting children's increased over-imitation regardless of action type.

Parental power distance interacted with action type (Median β = -0.36, 89%CI[-0.76, 0.03], pd = 92.77%), with children of parents reporting lower power distance showing similar imitation frequencies across action types, whereas children of parents reporting higher power distance exhibited larger differences.

We did not find supporting evidence for any effect of the cultural dimensions of uncertainty avoidance, humane orientation, and future orientation in parents on over-imitation in children (all pd < 90%).
